How Digital Payments Work and Getting Ready

Before you press any button, it helps to know what actually happens when money moves from one phone or card to another. This module explains the journey of a digital payment, compares it honestly with cash, maps every payment method you will meet in Nigeria, and walks you through the documents and settings you need to get started safely.

A digital payment is any payment where no physical cash changes hands. Instead, a number in one account goes down and a number in another account goes up. When you pay a tailor by bank transfer, pay a shop owner with your ATM card at a POS machine, or buy airtime by dialling a code, you are making a digital payment. The money is real. It is simply stored as a record in a bank or wallet company instead of as notes in your purse.

Many people feel nervous about digital payments because they cannot see the money travel. This lesson removes that mystery. Once you understand who holds your money and who passes the message along, you will know where to look when something goes wrong, and who to call.

The four parties in every payment
**The payer:** you, the person sending money. You give the instruction from a banking app, a USSD code, a card or a wallet app.

**The payer's bank or wallet provider:** the company that holds your money, for example a commercial bank, a microfinance bank or a mobile money company. It checks that you have enough money and that the instruction is really from you (your PIN, password or fingerprint).

**The payment network (the switch):** the shared road that connects different banks so they can talk to each other. In Nigeria, NIBSS (the Nigeria Inter-Bank Settlement System) runs the main instant transfer network, called NIP, that most bank-to-bank transfers travel on.
**The receiver's bank or wallet provider:** the company that holds the receiver's account. It adds the money to her balance and sends her an alert.

If you send money to someone who uses the same bank or the same wallet app as you, the network step is skipped: the company simply moves the record from your account to hers inside its own system. That is why same-bank transfers are often very fast.

Why the account name appears before you pay

When you type a 10-digit account number and choose a bank, your app usually shows the account holder's name before you confirm. This is called a **name enquiry**: your bank asks the receiver's bank, through the network, who owns that number. It is your most important safety check. If the name shown is not the person or business you expect, stop. Do not send because "the name is close enough".
Worked example: following ₦7,500 to a tailor
For example, Chioma in Enugu owes her tailor, Ada, ₦7,500 for sewing a dress. Chioma banks with one bank; Ada uses a different bank.
Chioma opens her banking app, taps Transfer, types Ada's 10-digit account number and selects Ada's bank.
The app shows the name "ADA N. OKAFOR". This matches the name Ada gave her, so Chioma continues.
She types 7500 as the amount and "Dress sewing balance" as the description (also called narration).
Chioma enters her 4-digit transaction PIN. Her bank checks her balance: she has ₦12,300, so the payment is allowed.
Her balance falls to ₦12,300 minus ₦7,500 = ₦4,800, plus any transfer charge her bank shows on the confirmation screen.
The message travels over the network to Ada's bank, which adds ₦7,500 to Ada's account and sends Ada an alert.
Chioma keeps the receipt screen as proof. Ada does not rely on a screenshot from Chioma: she opens her own app and sees ₦7,500 in her balance. That is the only real proof that money has arrived.

Words you will see often
**Debit:** money going out of your account.
**Credit:** money coming into your account.
**Narration or description:** the short note attached to a payment, for example "Rent October".

**Pending:** the instruction has been sent but has not finished. Do not send the same money again; wait and check.

When a POS machine prints "declined", when a transfer stays pending, or when an ATM does not give you cash, the question is always the same: which step in the chain failed, and which bank holds the record? Usually it is your own bank, the one whose app you use, that must help you first.

What digital payments change for a woman's money: control, records and reach

Many women in Nigeria earn and spend in small amounts every day: a market stall, a hair salon, a food business, a monthly contribution to a savings group. Cash is familiar and it works. But cash has hidden weaknesses. It can be stolen on the way home, borrowed without being returned, spent without anyone remembering where it went, and it leaves no record when you need to prove your income. Digital payments do not fix everything, but they change some of these things in useful ways.
A woman looking at money and charts on a screen
An account in your own name gives you a record and control that cash cannot.
Four things that change

**Control:** money in an account protected by your own PIN is harder for someone else to take or spend without your knowledge than cash in a box at home. You decide who knows the PIN, and the answer should be nobody.
**Records:** every transfer, POS payment and bill payment appears in your transaction history with a date, amount and description. This is a free notebook that keeps itself.
**Reach:** you can pay a supplier in another town, receive payment from a customer who saw your goods on WhatsApp, or send money to your mother in the village without travelling.
**Safety on the road:** carrying ₦150,000 in cash to buy stock is a risk. Paying the supplier by transfer means there is less cash to lose on a bus or in a crowded market.
Why records matter more than people think

When you apply for a loan from a microfinance bank or a cooperative, or join a grant programme, you are often asked how much your business earns. With cash, you can only guess. With a bank or wallet account, you can download a statement that shows money coming in month after month. That statement is evidence of a real business. It also helps you see, honestly, where your money goes.
Worked example: what a month of records shows
For example, Ngozi sells smoked fish in Onitsha. In one month she receives some payments by transfer and some in cash. She decides to add up only the transfers recorded in her app.
Week 1 transfers in: ₦38,000. Week 2: ₦41,500. Week 3: ₦29,000. Week 4: ₦45,500.
Her app also shows transfers out to her fish supplier: ₦60,000 and ₦55,000, a total of ₦115,000.
Money in minus money out for stock: ₦154,000 minus ₦115,000 = ₦39,000.
She cannot do the same calculation for her cash sales, because she wrote nothing down.

Ngozi sees that her digital records give her clear numbers for the part of the business that went through the app. She decides to ask more customers to pay by transfer so that her statement shows her true income.

Charges are real but visible

Some transfers, POS withdrawals, USSD sessions and card services carry a charge. The amounts change and differ between banks and apps, so this course does not quote them. The rule is simple: before you confirm, read the fee shown on the confirmation screen, and check your statement afterwards to see what was actually deducted.
Keeping control inside the family

An account only gives you control if it is truly yours. Open it in your own name, with your own phone number, and keep your PIN private, even from a husband, child or close friend. This is not about distrust; it is how banks expect accounts to be used. If someone else knows your PIN, the bank may treat their payments as your own. If you want to help a family member, send them money from your account; do not give them access to it.

Digital payments also help when you save with others. Many savings groups (ajo, esusu, adashe) now collect contributions by transfer. Each member's transfer shows in the collector's statement with a date and name, which reduces arguments about who paid and when. Ask that the group agrees one account for collections and that members put their name and the month in the narration.

The hidden costs of cash

People often say cash is free. It is not. To have cash, you may first need to withdraw it from an ATM or a POS agent, and the agent charges you for that service. You may pay transport to reach a bank or agent. You spend time. You may receive a damaged or fake note. And if cash is lost or stolen, it is gone, with no bank to call. When you compare, include all of these, not only the bank charge you can see on a screen.
Worked example: paying a wholesaler ₦80,000
For example, Amina runs a food stall in Kaduna and needs to pay a rice wholesaler ₦80,000. She has the money in her bank account. She compares two options using her own real costs.

Option A, cash: she must withdraw ₦80,000 from a POS agent near her house. The agent tells her his charge for that amount; for this example, suppose he says ₦1,600 (a made-up number for practice; real charges vary). She also pays ₦500 transport each way to the wholesaler with the cash: ₦1,000.
Cost of option A: ₦1,600 + ₦1,000 = ₦2,600, plus the risk of carrying ₦80,000 on a bus.

Option B, transfer: she transfers ₦80,000 from her banking app. Her app's confirmation screen shows the transfer charge before she confirms; for this example, suppose it shows ₦50 (again a practice number).
She still travels to collect the rice, so transport is ₦1,000 in both options. Cost of option B: ₦50 + ₦1,000 = ₦1,050.
Difference: ₦2,600 minus ₦1,050 = ₦1,550 in favour of the transfer, and she carries no cash.

Using the real numbers she sees on her own screens, Amina can make this comparison for any payment. Here the transfer is cheaper and safer, and she gets a record. She asks the wholesaler for his account details in person and checks the name on her app before paying.

Planning a weekly mix

Most households end up with a mix. A common pattern is: keep a small amount of cash for daily market items and transport, and use transfers or cards for rent, school fees, suppliers, bills and anything above a level you choose. Decide your own level. For example, you might decide that any payment above ₦10,000 goes by transfer. Write the rule down and keep it for a month, then review.
Write your cash rule, for example: "Cash only for payments below ₦10,000 and for sellers without accounts."
Withdraw cash once or twice a week, not every day, to reduce charges and trips.
Pay everything else digitally and keep receipts in a phone folder or note.
At the end of the week, count how much cash you withdrew and what it was used for.
Notice that choosing well is about the situation, not about which method is more modern. A sensible mix keeps you flexible when the network fails and protected when the amounts grow.

Bank account or wallet: what is the difference?

A **bank account** is held by a commercial bank or a microfinance bank. A **mobile money wallet** is an account held by a company licensed to run mobile money services. Some popular apps that people call wallets are actually run by licensed microfinance banks: for example, Moniepoint states on its website that Moniepoint Microfinance Bank is authorised and regulated by the Central Bank of Nigeria and that deposits are insured by the Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation (NDIC). For any app, look for this kind of statement at the bottom of its website or in the app's About or Legal section before you keep money there.

Both bank accounts and wallets give you a 10-digit account number that others can transfer to, and both can usually send to and receive from any other bank. For daily payments the experience feels the same. What matters for you is: is the provider licensed, is your account protected by your own PIN, and can you reach customer support when something fails?

Worked example: picking a method for three payments
For example, Funmi owns a small provisions shop in Ibadan. She has a smartphone, a bank account and a wallet app, but data is sometimes finished. This week she has three payments to make.
Payment 1: ₦45,000 to her drinks supplier in another area. Large and far away, so she uses an app transfer and checks the supplier's account name before confirming.
Payment 2: ₦2,000 airtime on Wednesday evening when her data has run out. She uses her bank's USSD code on the same phone, which works without data.
Payment 3: ₦18,500 for cooking gas at a station with a POS machine. She pays with her debit card and PIN, watching the amount on the screen.
Total paid digitally this week: ₦45,000 + ₦2,000 + ₦18,500 = ₦65,500.
She notes that all three appear in her bank statement, even though she used three different methods.
Funmi used the method that fitted each situation, and every payment still came from, and was recorded in, her own account.
Where your money actually sits

Notice from the example that the method is only the door. The money is in your account. A card, a USSD code, an app and a QR scan are all different doors into the same room. This matters for safety: if someone gets through any one door with your PIN or password, they can reach the whole balance. Protect every door with the same care.

**Pay with transfer at a POS:** some POS terminals show an account number so a customer can pay by transfer instead of card.
**Direct debit or standing order:** an instruction that lets a bank pay a fixed amount on a set date, for example a monthly contribution.

A good set-up prevents most later problems. Many failed payments, blocked accounts and stolen balances start with a weak PIN, an old phone number linked to the account, or an account opened through someone else. This lesson is your setup checklist. Take your time with it.
A person logging in securely on a phone
Setting up correctly once protects every payment you make afterwards.
The numbers that identify you

**NIN (National Identification Number):** an 11-digit number issued by the National Identity Management Commission when you enrol for the national ID. Banks and wallet providers use it to confirm who you are.

**BVN (Bank Verification Number):** an 11-digit number linked to your fingerprints and face, captured at a bank. One BVN covers all your bank accounts in Nigeria. It helps banks know that the same person owns several accounts.
**Account number:** a 10-digit number for each account. This is the number you share so people can pay you.
**Phone number:** the number linked to your account. Alerts, one-time passwords (OTPs) and USSD access all depend on it.
Share your account number, never your PIN or OTP

Your account number is safe to share with people who need to pay you. Your BVN and NIN should only be given to a bank or provider you have chosen, through its official app, website or branch. Your PIN, password and any OTP must never be shared with anyone, including someone who says they work for your bank.
Account levels and limits

Banks and wallets in Nigeria use levels (often called tiers) for accounts. An account opened with only basic details sits on a low level with lower limits on how much you can receive, keep or send in a day. When you add more identification, such as your BVN, NIN, a photo and proof of address, you can upgrade to a higher level with higher limits. The exact limits are set by the Central Bank of Nigeria and applied by each provider, and they change from time to time, so this course does not quote them. Find your own: open your app, go to Profile or Account, and look for Account level, Tier or Limits.

Setting up an app safely
Open the Play Store or App Store and search for your bank or wallet by name. Check the publisher matches the real company and look at how many downloads and reviews it has.
Install it yourself on your own phone. Do not let an agent install it on their phone for you.

Worked example: choosing a PIN that is hard to guess
For example, Halima in Kano is setting her transaction PIN. She was born in 1986, her phone number ends in 4471 and her shop is at No. 12.
She rejects 1986 (birth year), 4471 (end of phone number) and 1212 (shop number repeated), because a thief who finds her ID card, her phone or her shop could guess them.
She rejects 1234, 0000 and 2580 (the straight line down the middle of the keypad), because these are common, easy patterns that a thief would try early.
There are 10 x 10 x 10 x 10 = 10,000 possible 4-digit PINs. A random choice is very hard to guess within the few attempts allowed before the account locks.
She picks four digits from something only she knows and that is not written on any document, and practises typing it five times.
She does not write the PIN on her card, in her phone notes or on paper in her bag.
Halima's PIN is not linked to any information a stranger can find, so even if her phone or ID is stolen, the PIN cannot be guessed easily.
If you share a phone or have an old number

If you share a phone with family members, do not stay logged in to your banking app, and use the app's own password or fingerprint lock. If the phone number on your account belongs to a SIM you no longer use, alerts and OTPs go to whoever now has that number. Visit your bank with a valid ID to change it. This is one of the most important fixes you can make.
Turn on alerts and know your support channels

Make sure you receive alerts for every transaction, by SMS, email or app notification. Alerts tell you quickly if money leaves your account without your knowledge. Save your bank's official customer care number in your contacts under the bank's name, copied from the bank's website or the back of your card. When you need help, you will call that saved number, not a number you find in a social media comment.

USSD is the service you use when you dial a short code that starts with * and ends with #, like the codes you use to check airtime. Banks and some wallet providers use USSD so that you can check your balance, transfer money and buy airtime from any phone, even a basic phone with no internet. In places where data is expensive or the network is weak, USSD is often the most reliable way to pay.

How USSD works

When you dial a USSD code, your phone opens a live session with your bank through your mobile network. Menus appear on the screen as text. You reply by typing a number and pressing Send. The session only lasts a short time, so if you take too long, it closes and you start again. Because it runs over the voice network rather than the internet, it works without data. It only works with the SIM card registered to your account, which is part of its security.
Getting your bank's code and registering
Find your bank's official USSD code: it is often printed on the back of the bank card, on the bank's website, or displayed in the branch. Do not use a code someone sends you.
Make sure the SIM in your phone is the number registered with your bank account.
Dial the code. The first time, you are usually asked to register by entering some digits from your debit card or account and creating a USSD PIN.
Choose a USSD PIN that is different from your card PIN and not easy to guess.
Do a balance check first. It is the easiest way to confirm that everything works.
USSD has charges

Banks and mobile networks may charge for each USSD session, usually deducted from your airtime or bank account. The amount is not the same everywhere and changes over time. Watch for the charge notice that appears on screen or by SMS, and check your statement.

If you sell anything, you will receive more transfers than you send. Receiving money is where traders lose the most to tricks, because the pressure comes at the busiest moment: a customer in a hurry, a queue behind him, a phone held up with "I have sent it". A calm routine protects you without being rude to honest customers.
A person happily receiving a payment notification

The one rule: check your own balance

An SMS alert can be faked, a screenshot can be edited, and a receipt can be old. Your balance inside your own app, or by your bank's USSD balance check, comes directly from your bank. Before you release goods, check it. For busy shops, a wallet app with instant in-app notifications helps, but still open the history and look for the exact amount and name.
Tell the customer your account number and provider name clearly, written on a card.

"Thank you, please give me one minute to see it on my side. As soon as it shows, I will pack your goods." Honest customers understand. Someone who becomes angry or rushes you at this point is a warning sign.
End-of-day matching

At closing time, compare what you sold with what you received. This catches payments that never arrived, double payments, and mistakes in giving change. You need two lists: your sales notebook (or a simple list on your phone) and your app's history for today.
Worked example: closing the day at a fabric stall
For example, Aisha sells fabric at a market in Ilorin. Her notebook shows six sales paid by transfer today: ₦8,500, ₦12,000, ₦4,500, ₦15,000, ₦6,000 and ₦9,500.

Difference: ₦55,500 minus ₦49,500 = ₦6,000. One sale is missing.
She checks her notebook: the ₦6,000 sale was the woman who showed a screenshot when the stall was busy.
She notes the customer's name and phone number from her notebook and, next time, will always check before releasing goods.
Aisha finds the exact missing payment the same day, while the details are fresh, and she can follow it up calmly with the customer instead of discovering a gap at the end of the month.

POS stands for point of sale: the place where a sale happens. A POS terminal is the small handheld machine with a card slot, a keypad and a printer that shops and agents use to accept card payments. Most terminals today are small Android devices that connect through a SIM card or Wi-Fi. They are supplied to businesses by banks and payment companies, and each one is linked to the business owner's account.
A bank card
Your debit card is the key; the POS terminal is the lock that asks your bank for permission.
Who is involved in a card payment
**You, the cardholder,** with a debit card issued by your bank, carrying a card scheme logo such as Verve, Mastercard or Visa.
**The issuer:** your bank, which holds your money and decides whether to approve the payment.
**The merchant:** the shop or agent with the POS terminal.
**The acquirer or terminal provider:** the bank or payment company that gave the merchant the terminal and pays the merchant.
**The switch and card scheme:** the networks that carry the request from the terminal to your bank and back.

You enter PIN privately
Request sent to your bank
Bank approves or declines
Receipt prints, both credited
The whole round trip usually takes seconds; a failure at any step should mean no debit or a reversal.

When you insert your card, the chip on the card talks to the terminal. You check the amount and enter your PIN. The terminal sends a request through the networks to your bank. Your bank checks your PIN, your balance and its fraud checks, then sends back "approved" or "declined". The terminal prints a receipt. Your account is debited and the merchant's account is credited, usually minus a service charge that the merchant pays to the terminal provider.

Worked example: checking two receipts at a supermarket

For example, Ruth pays for groceries at a supermarket in Lagos. The cashier enters ₦23,750. The first attempt prints a receipt, then the cashier says "network" and tries again, and a second receipt prints.
Ruth reads the first receipt: status DECLINED, amount ₦23,750. A declined receipt means the bank did not approve it.
She reads the second receipt: status APPROVED, amount ₦23,750, same terminal ID, a different RRN.
She opens her banking app before leaving. She sees one debit of ₦23,750, not two.
Had she seen two debits, she would add them: ₦23,750 x 2 = ₦47,500, and the extra ₦23,750 would need to be reversed.
She keeps both receipts in her purse, because the declined one proves the first attempt failed.
Ruth confirms she was charged once. If the app had shown a second debit, she would already have both receipts with the RRNs and terminal ID needed for a complaint to her bank.
Card payment or cash-out?

The same POS terminal can do two different things. In a **purchase**, you pay a shop for goods with your card. In a **withdrawal** or **cash-out** at a POS agent, the agent debits your card for an amount and hands you that cash, and usually charges you a fee for the service, which may be added on top or taken from the cash. Always agree the total amount and the agent's charge before you insert your card, and check the amount on the screen before entering your PIN.
Pay with transfer at a POS

Some terminals can display an account number for the customer to pay by transfer instead of card. The same rule applies: the merchant should confirm the credit on the terminal or app before releasing goods, and you should keep your transfer receipt.
Chip, PIN and the magnetic stripe

Your card has a gold or silver **chip** and a black **magnetic stripe** on the back. The chip is much harder to copy than the stripe, which is why terminals ask you to insert the card chip-first rather than swipe it. If a cashier or agent says the chip is not working and wants to swipe instead, be careful: try another terminal or pay another way, and ask your bank to replace a card whose chip has stopped working.

Keep receipts for card payments until you have checked your statement at the end of the month. A small envelope in your bag or a photo folder on your phone works well. When there is a problem, the receipt turns a long argument into a quick check by your bank.

Your PIN is the key

Your card PIN is a 4-digit number that proves to your bank that you are the cardholder. If someone sees it and later gets your card, they can empty your account. Cover the keypad every time, even with people you know. Never say your PIN aloud, never give it to a cashier to type for you, and never write it on the card or in its sleeve. If you think someone has seen it, change it at an ATM or in your banking app as soon as you can.
The card swap

A dishonest person can take your card, keep it out of your sight for a moment and return a similar-looking card. With the PIN they watched you type, they then use your real card. Always check the name and last four digits on the card you get back.
Worked example: catching a wrong amount
For example, Blessing is buying a gas refill and some groceries in Owerri. The agreed total is ₦18,400. She is in a hurry.
The cashier enters the amount and turns the terminal towards her. The screen shows ₦184,000.00.
Blessing counts the digits before the decimal point: 184000 has six digits, but ₦18,400 should have five: 18400.
She does not enter her PIN. She says calmly: "The amount is wrong, it should be eighteen thousand four hundred."
The cashier cancels and enters it again. The screen now shows ₦18,400.00.
Blessing covers the keypad, enters her PIN, and the receipt prints APPROVED, ₦18,400.
Had she not checked, she could have been debited ₦184,000 minus ₦18,400 = ₦165,600 more than she owed, and had to wait for a complaint to be resolved.
Ten seconds of checking saved Blessing a very large mistake and a long complaint process. She now reads the screen aloud every time.

An ATM (automated teller machine) lets you withdraw cash, check your balance, change your PIN and sometimes transfer money, using your card and PIN. It is quicker than a bank queue. ATMs feel intimidating to some people because the screens move fast and there is often a queue behind you. With a little preparation, you can use one confidently.
A bank building
ATMs at or inside your own bank branch are usually the safest to use.
Before you go
Check your balance in your app first, so you know what you can withdraw.
Decide the amount. ATMs pay in the notes they hold, so ask for a round amount, for example in thousands.
Prefer an ATM inside or at the front of a bank branch, in daylight, where there is security.
Have your card ready before you reach the machine so you do not search your bag there.
Withdrawing cash, step by step
Look at the card slot and keypad. If anything looks loose, glued, extra-thick or different from other ATMs, do not use it.
Insert your card as shown by the picture on the machine.
Choose your language, then cover the keypad and enter your PIN.
Choose Withdrawal, then the account type (usually Savings or Current, as your account is).
Choose or type the amount. If a fee notice appears, read it, then accept or cancel.
Take your card first, then your cash, then your receipt if you asked for one. Count the cash discreetly, put it away before you leave, and check the debit in your app.

Taking your card back before walking away is the step people most often forget.
ATM fees

Using another bank's ATM may carry a charge, and rules on ATM fees are set by the Central Bank of Nigeria and change over time. This course does not quote amounts. Many machines show a fee notice on screen before you confirm; read it, and check your statement afterwards.
Worked example: planning one withdrawal instead of four
For example, Kemi in Ibadan used to withdraw ₦5,000 at a time from a nearby ATM belonging to a different bank, four times a week. She wants to cut the trips and any charges.
Her weekly cash use is 4 x ₦5,000 = ₦20,000.
She checks her past month in her app: each of those withdrawals showed a separate charge line. Four withdrawals a week means four charge lines a week.
She lists what she really needs cash for: transport about ₦7,000, market items about ₦10,000, and small extras about ₦3,000. Total: ₦7,000 + ₦10,000 + ₦3,000 = ₦20,000.
She decides on one ₦20,000 withdrawal on Monday from her own bank's ATM on the way to work, and pays bigger items by transfer or card.
She keeps ₦10,000 in her purse and ₦10,000 at home, so she does not carry it all at once.
Kemi makes one trip instead of four, reduces the number of charge lines on her statement, and still has the same cash for the week.
Traps to avoid
**Helpful strangers:** never accept help from anyone at an ATM, even if they say they work there. If you need help, go inside the bank or call your bank.
**Shoulder surfers:** people standing too close to watch your PIN. Ask them to step back, or cancel and leave.

**Card trapping:** a device inside the slot that holds your card. If your card is stuck, do not walk away to "get help" from someone nearby; call your bank's official number from where you stand and block the card.
**Skimmers:** devices fitted over the slot or keypad to copy your card details. Check the machine before use.
Card kept by the machine?

Stay at the machine, call your bank's official customer care number saved in your phone, and ask them to block the card immediately. Then report to the branch. Do not type your PIN again because someone tells you to.
If the ATM does not give you cash
Changing your PIN and other ATM services

Most ATMs also let you change your card PIN, which you should do if you think anyone has seen it. Choose PIN Change from the menu, enter your old PIN, then your new PIN twice. Some ATMs also offer balance enquiry and mini-statements. A balance enquiry is useful when you have no data and your phone is not registered for USSD, but remember that the machine may charge for it too, so read the screen.

Sometimes the screen says the transaction is complete but no cash comes out, or only part of the cash. Do not leave immediately: note the ATM location and its number (often on a sticker on the machine), the time, and the amount. Check your app. If you were debited, report it to your own bank, even if the ATM belonged to another bank. The next lesson shows you how to write that complaint.

A POS agent offers banking services to people in a neighbourhood: cash withdrawals, deposits by transfer, bill payments and airtime, using a POS terminal and a phone. In many areas, agents are the nearest place to get cash. It can be a useful business, but it handles a lot of money every day, so it needs discipline, good records and strong security.
A small shop front with a person serving customers
A POS agent business is a small shop whose stock is cash and account balance.
Getting a terminal
Choose a licensed provider. Banks and payment companies such as Moniepoint and Opay offer agent terminals. Check the provider's licence statement as you learned in Module 2.
Apply through the provider's official app, website or office, not through a stranger selling terminals on social media.

Provide what the provider asks for. This usually includes your BVN, NIN, a valid ID, your phone number and your business location; some providers also ask for business registration. Each provider sets its own list.
Ask the provider, in writing, for its fee schedule: what it charges you per transaction, any terminal cost or caution fee, and when money settles into your account.
Ask which Central Bank of Nigeria agent banking rules apply to you, including any limits on how much cash a customer may withdraw. Follow them exactly.
Register your business name with the Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC) if you plan to grow; it helps with bank relationships.
Understanding float

Your **float** is the money you need to run the business, held in two places: **cash** in your drawer and **e-value**, meaning money in your agent account. When a customer withdraws, you give out cash and your account balance goes up. When a customer gives you cash to transfer for them, your cash goes up and your account balance goes down. Your total float stays roughly the same; it simply moves between the two places. If either side runs out, you cannot serve the next customer.

Each service moves money from one side of your float to the other, so watch both.
Worked example: one morning's float

For example, Zainab runs a POS stand in Jos. She starts the day with ₦150,000 cash and ₦100,000 in her agent account: a total float of ₦250,000. These are her own working numbers, not provider figures.
Customer 3 gives her ₦30,000 cash to transfer to his brother: cash ₦80,000 + ₦30,000 = ₦110,000; account ₦170,000 minus ₦30,000 = ₦140,000.
Check: ₦110,000 cash + ₦140,000 account = ₦250,000, the same total float as the morning, before her charges and the provider's fees.
Her record book shows the service charges she collected from customers this morning came to ₦2,400 in cash, kept in a separate envelope so she can see her earnings.
Zainab's float balances, and her charges are separate, so at closing she knows exactly what she earned. When her cash drops low, she plans a trip to the bank to change e-value back into cash.

Never give out cash until the terminal prints APPROVED and your app shows the credit. Keep most cash out of sight in a locked box, and do not count large sums in public. Pricing your charges honestly

Agents set their own customer charges in many areas, within any rules the provider or regulator sets. Display your charges clearly on a board so customers can see them before they start. Check your provider's fee schedule so that what you charge covers the provider's fee, your time, transport to the bank for cash, and a fair profit. Honest, visible prices bring customers back.

The most stressful case is when your account is debited but the receiver does not get the money, or the ATM gives no cash. Many of these are reversed automatically. When they are not, a clear complaint with the right evidence gets them fixed far faster than shouting at a cashier or agent.

Worked example: a POS cash-out that failed

For example, Ebere in Aba goes to a POS agent to withdraw ₦30,000 for her shop. The agent's terminal prints DECLINED, and no cash is given. A minute later, Ebere receives a debit alert of ₦30,000 from her bank.
Ebere does not let the agent try again. She asks for the declined receipt and takes a photo of it: it shows the agent's business name, terminal ID, ₦30,000, the time, RRN and STAN.
She checks her app: one debit of ₦30,000 at the time on the receipt, and no reversal yet.
That evening she still has no reversal. She calls her bank's official number from the back of her card and reports a failed POS withdrawal, giving the date, time, amount, terminal ID and RRN.
The bank gives her a complaint reference number. She writes it in her notebook with the date and the name of the staff member.
She sets a reminder to check her app daily and follow up with the reference number if the money has not returned.

When the ₦30,000 reversal arrives, she notes the date and checks her balance: if her balance before was ₦52,000, after the debit it was ₦52,000 minus ₦30,000 = ₦22,000, and after the reversal it is back to ₦22,000 + ₦30,000 = ₦52,000.
Because Ebere had the receipt, references and a complaint number, her bank could trace the exact transaction, and she could confirm her balance was fully restored.
Writing your complaint

Use your bank's in-app support, official email or customer care line. Keep it short and complete, for example: "On 14 March at 2:10 pm I attempted a POS withdrawal of ₦30,000 at [agent name], terminal ID [number], RRN [number]. The terminal printed DECLINED and I received no cash, but my account was debited ₦30,000. Please reverse the debit. My account number is [number]." Ask for a complaint reference number and keep it.
Beware fake "customer care"

When you post about a failed transaction on social media, fake accounts may reply offering to help and ask for your PIN, OTP or a "reactivation" payment. Real banks never ask for your PIN or OTP. Use only the official contact numbers on your card or the bank's website.
If your bank does not resolve it

If your bank does not resolve your complaint within the time it gives you, ask to escalate within the bank, quoting your reference number. If it is still not resolved, you can escalate to the Central Bank of Nigeria's consumer protection channel, which handles complaints against banks and other financial institutions it regulates. You will need your complaint reference from the bank and your evidence. Check the CBN's official website for the current complaint process.

Tricks aimed at POS agents and sellers
**The busy-time screenshot:** a customer shows a transfer receipt when the queue is long and leaves with cash or goods. Defence: check your own app history before releasing anything.

**The "reversal" after delivery:** a customer pays, collects, then claims to his bank that the transaction failed. Defence: keep the APPROVED receipt and your record book entry with the RRN, so you can answer your provider's dispute request.

**The fake staff visit:** someone says they are from your terminal provider and needs to take or "update" your terminal, or asks for your login. Defence: call the provider's official number before handing anything over.
The recovery trick

When a transaction fails, people often post their complaint on social media and tag their bank. Within minutes, accounts with the bank's logo reply: "Sorry for the inconvenience, send us a DM with your account details." They then ask for a PIN, an OTP, or a "reversal fee". These are not your bank. Real banks do not ask for your PIN or OTP and do not charge you to return your own money. Use only the contact details printed on your card or on the bank's official website.

Any request that pushes you to act fast is a reason to slow down.
Worked example: the help at the ATM
For example, Comfort is withdrawing ₦15,000 at an ATM outside a shopping plaza in Uyo in the evening. The machine seems to take a long time and her card does not come out.
A young man behind her says the machine always does this and tells her to press Cancel and type her PIN again while he holds the slot.
Comfort recognises the pattern from this course: a stuck card plus a helpful stranger asking for her PIN.
She steps back from the keypad, does not re-enter her PIN, and says she will call her bank.
She calls the customer care number saved in her phone and asks them to block the card immediately. The bank confirms the block.
She checks her app: no ₦15,000 debit, and no other debits. She reports the ATM at the bank branch the next morning and requests a replacement card.
Even if a device had trapped her card, it is now useless to anyone, and her balance is safe. Comfort lost a card, which can be replaced, not her savings.
Three things no genuine person will ask for
Your PIN. Your OTP. A fee to receive or recover your own money. Anyone who asks for one of these, whatever they say, should be treated as a scammer.
Protecting your stall from disputes

If you run a POS stand or accept cards in a shop, your provider may contact you when a customer disputes a payment with his bank. Answer quickly through the provider's official app or email, and send what you have: the APPROVED receipt or its RRN, the time, and your record book entry showing the cash given or goods delivered. A clear record usually settles the matter. Without one, you may lose the money even when you were honest.
If you think you have been tricked
Block your card or freeze your account at once, using your app or the bank's official number.
Change your PIN and app password from a phone you trust.
Report to your bank with the date, time, amount and any receipts, and get a complaint reference.
Tell your family or market group what happened so they recognise the same trick.
Never pay anyone who offers to recover the money for a fee.

There is no shame in being targeted. These tricks are designed by people who practise them every day. What matters is acting quickly, because the faster your bank knows, the better the chance of stopping further loss.
Card swaps, PIN watching and ATM helpers all rely on taking your card or PIN out of your control.
Sellers must confirm credits in their own app and keep APPROVED receipts for disputes.
Fake "customer care" replies on social media are a common recovery trick.
No genuine person asks for your PIN, OTP or a fee to return your money.

Your money is protected by a few secrets and one device: your phone. If someone gets your phone and one of your secrets, they can move your money. This lesson helps you lock both, and gives you a plan for the worst day, when your phone is stolen on a bus or your bag is snatched at the market.

An OTP is a short code sent to your phone by SMS or email to confirm an action. Always read the whole OTP message. It often says what the code is for, for example "to log in on a new device" or "to pay ₦45,000 to an online shop". If you did not start that action, someone else did. Do not give the code to anyone, and call your bank.
Lock your phone and apps
Set a screen lock on your phone: PIN, pattern, fingerprint or face. Avoid simple patterns like an L or Z shape.
Turn on the app lock or fingerprint login in every banking and wallet app.
Turn off message previews on the lock screen for SMS, so OTPs are not visible when the phone is locked. Look in Settings, Notifications, Lock screen.
Keep your phone's software and apps updated from the official store.
Set lower daily transfer limits in your banking app if it lets you, so a thief cannot move everything at once.
Write down your phone's IMEI number (dial *#06#) and keep it at home; it helps when reporting a stolen phone.

Bank daily limits
App lock and PIN
Phone screen lock
Private secrets, never shared
Each layer stops a thief who got past the one below; the base is keeping your secrets private.
Worked example: phone stolen on a bus
For example, Folake's phone is snatched from her hand on a bus in Lagos at 6:15 pm. It has her banking app, a wallet app and the SIM linked to both accounts.

6:20 pm: she borrows a phone from a trusted colleague and calls her bank on the official number written on the card in her purse. She asks them to block mobile and USSD banking and her card if it was in the phone case.
6:30 pm: she calls her wallet provider's official number (written in her notebook) and asks the same.
6:45 pm: she calls her mobile network to block the SIM so no one can receive her OTPs or use USSD.
Next morning: she checks her accounts from a bank branch or a trusted device. She sees no debits after 6:15 pm.
She buys a replacement SIM with the same number at her network's official outlet, using her ID, then reinstalls her apps and sets new passwords and PINs.

Within half an hour, all three routes into Folake's money were closed. Because she had her bank and wallet numbers written down away from her phone, she did not need the stolen phone to make the calls.
Keep your emergency numbers on paper too

Write your bank's and wallet provider's official customer care numbers, and your account numbers (not your PINs), on a small card kept at home and another in your purse. If the phone is gone, you still know who to call.
Signs your account may be at risk
You receive an OTP you did not request.
You get an alert for a login on a new device you do not own.
Your phone suddenly shows "No service" or "SIM not registered" in a place where it normally works, which can mean someone has taken over your number.
A debit appears that you did not make.

Any of these is a reason to call your bank's official number immediately and ask them to freeze mobile and USSD banking while you check. It is better to make a call that turns out to be unnecessary than to wait.
What is safe to share
**Safe to share:** your account number and account name, with people who need to pay you.
**Share carefully:** your phone number and your BVN or NIN, only with providers you have chosen, through official channels.
**Never share:** PINs, passwords, OTPs, photos of the front and back of your card, or your phone unlocked to someone who wants to "help" you with the app.
PINs, passwords and OTPs are for you alone; read every OTP message to see what it approves.

If your phone is stolen, block bank, wallet and SIM within the hour.
Keep official support numbers on paper as well as in your phone.

Every digital payment you make leaves a line in your statement. That means you already have a budget record without writing anything. Most people never look at it. This lesson shows you how to turn a month of statement lines into a clear picture of where your money went, and then to make one or two practical decisions.
A person reviewing a budget with charts
Your statement is a ready-made spending record.
Getting your statement
Open your banking or wallet app and find Transactions, History or Statement.
Choose a date range: the first to the last day of last month.
View it on screen or download it as a PDF. Save it in a phone folder named by month.
If you use more than one account, get a statement from each. Moving money between your own accounts is not spending; mark those lines so you do not count them twice.
Sort into a few groups

Do not use too many groups. Five or six are enough for a first month. A simple set is: food and household, transport, airtime and data, bills (electricity, TV, rent), business stock, and charges. Go through the debits one by one and write each amount under its group. Many apps now group spending automatically; check their grouping, because they often guess wrongly.
Worked example: Hadiza's October statement
For example, Hadiza is a caterer in Abuja. She downloads her October statement and sorts the debits into groups. She ignores two transfers to her own savings account.
Business stock (rice, oil, chicken): ₦65,000 + ₦48,000 = ₦113,000.
Airtime and data: 9 payments of ₦1,000 and 2 of ₦3,500 = ₦9,000 + ₦7,000 = ₦16,000.
Bills: electricity tokens ₦10,000 + ₦8,000 and TV ₦6,000 = ₦24,000.
Transport by transfer to drivers: ₦12,400.
Charges lines (transfer, SMS alert and card charges as shown in the statement): she adds them and gets ₦1,850.
Hadiza sees that airtime and data cost her ₦16,000 in small top-ups. She decides to buy one monthly data plan instead of many small ones and to compare its price in her app next month.

Sort into groups
Total each group
Pick one change
Check next month
Repeating this review every month turns your statement into a budgeting habit.
What to look for
**Many small payments** to the same place, such as airtime or snacks, that add up to a large monthly sum.
**Charges:** transfer fees, SMS alert charges, card maintenance and USSD charges. Add them up; you may decide to change how you pay.
**Repeated subscriptions** you forgot about.
**Debits you do not recognise.** Report these to your bank immediately; they may be fraud.
A debit you do not recognise
If you find a payment you did not make, do not wait for the end of your review. Block your card or app, and report it to your bank with the date, amount and description shown on the statement.

Also look at money coming in. If you sell, the credits in your statement show which weeks were busy and which were slow. Mark the slow weeks on a calendar. Next year, you can plan bigger costs, such as restocking or school fees, away from those slow weeks.
Turning the review into action

Choose one group where you want to spend less and set a simple limit for next month, for example "airtime and data: no more than ₦10,000". Then use a digital tool to help. Many banking and wallet apps have a savings feature, sometimes called a pocket, target or vault, where you can move money aside on a set day. Before using one, read its terms in the app: whether you can withdraw any time, whether there is a penalty for early withdrawal, and who holds the money.
Decision

Note the limit in your phone and check the statement weekly
Save a fixed amount
Savings pocket or target in your app, or a standing transfer to a separate account
Reduce charges
Use the payment method with the lowest charge shown on the fee screens you compared
Separate business money
A second account only for business, as in the next lesson
Cash spending counts too

Your statement only shows digital payments. Cash withdrawals appear as one line each, but the cash itself was spent on many things. For your first review, put cash withdrawals in their own group, and if you want more detail, keep a small note of cash spending for the same month.

Repeat the review at the start of every month. After three months, you will know your real spending pattern better than any guess, and you will be able to plan school fees, rent and stock with confidence.

A small business in Nigeria can collect payments in three main digital ways: direct transfer to its account, card payments through a POS terminal, and online payments through a payment gateway such as Paystack, which lets customers pay by card, bank transfer or other options through a link or checkout page. Each has its own cost and its own best use.

Paystack publishes its pricing on its official website. When this course was checked in October 2026, the page stated that local transactions cost **1.5% + ₦100**, that the **₦100 is waived for transactions under ₦2,500**, and that the fee is **capped at ₦2,000**. International card payments cost 3.9% + ₦100. Prices change, so always check the pricing page before you rely on these figures.
Worked example: what Paystack would charge on three orders

For example, Ifeoma sells hair products and takes orders on WhatsApp. She is thinking of sending Paystack payment links to new customers. She works out the fee on three typical orders using the published local rate.
Order A, ₦2,000 (under ₦2,500, so the ₦100 is waived): 1.5% of ₦2,000 = ₦30. Fee ₦30. She receives ₦2,000 minus ₦30 = ₦1,970.
Order C, ₦200,000 (a salon's bulk order): 1.5% of ₦200,000 = ₦3,000, plus ₦100 = ₦3,100. This is above the ₦2,000 cap, so the fee is ₦2,000. She receives ₦200,000 minus ₦2,000 = ₦198,000.
As a share of the order: ₦30 is 1.5% of Order A, ₦325 is about 2.2% of Order B, and ₦2,000 is 1% of Order C.
Ifeoma decides to keep direct transfer for regular customers, and to use payment links for new customers who want to pay by card, adding the expected fee into her pricing for those orders.

Setting up a payment gateway
Go to the gateway's official website and create a business account with your own email and phone number.
Complete the business verification it requests. Paystack, like other gateways, asks for business and identity details before you can receive live payments; follow its on-screen list.
Add the bank account where your money will be settled. Use a business account in your name or your business name.
Create a payment page or link for a product or a fixed amount, and test it with a small payment.
Share the link only from your official WhatsApp Business or social media account, so customers know it is yours.
Links can be faked too

Scammers copy payment pages. Tell your customers the exact name that will appear on your payment page, and never ask them to send card details or OTPs to you on WhatsApp. A proper gateway collects card details on its own secure page.
Telling customers how to pay

Whatever methods you choose, write them clearly in one place: your WhatsApp Business profile, your catalogue, or a small board at your stall. For example: "Pay by transfer to [account name], [account number], [provider]; card payments accepted at the stall; new online customers may pay by card through our payment link." Clear payment instructions reduce mistakes, make you look professional, and make it harder for anyone to slip in a different account number.

Record how each order was paid in your sales book. At the end of the month you can see how much came through each method and what each method cost you in fees. That tells you whether a method is worth keeping.
Keep business money separate

Open a separate account just for business. Ask customers to pay into it, pay suppliers from it, and pay yourself a fixed amount into your personal account each week or month. This one habit makes your statement a clean record of sales and costs, which you need for pricing, for loans, and for knowing if the business is really making a profit.

Confidence with digital payments comes from repetition. Each safe transfer, each careful POS payment and each statement review makes the next one easier. This final lesson helps you turn the course into a 30-day plan that you will actually follow, and gives you the evidence you need for your certificate.

**Three payment types:** for example one app transfer, one USSD transaction and one card payment at a POS, each done with the safe routine.

Week 2: pays her beans supplier by app transfer, buys airtime by USSD, pays for gas with her card at a POS, saving each receipt. In: ₦24,500; out: ₦19,000.

Your weekly check should take ten minutes. Open your history, add money in and money out, write the two numbers in your table, and note one thing you learned. A short habit you keep beats a long one you abandon.
Helping another woman start

One of the best ways to fix what you have learned is to teach it. Choose one woman, perhaps a sister, a neighbour or a member of your savings group, and help her with one thing: checking the account name before a transfer, covering her PIN, or saving her bank's official number. Do not ask for her PIN or handle her phone for her; guide her with words while she does it herself. That way she learns, and her account stays private.
When the plan slips

Most people miss a week at some point: a sick child, a busy market season, a broken phone. Do not restart from the beginning. Fill in what you can from your app history, which keeps the record for you, and continue with the next week's focus. The statement is still there when you are ready, so a missed week can always be caught up in one sitting.

At the end of the 30 days, compare your measures with where you started in Module 1. Look back at your cash-to-digital list from Lesson 1.2 and tick the payments you have moved. Write one sentence about what you can now do that you could not do before. That sentence, with your receipts and tables, is the heart of your capstone project.

Cover the keypad. Never let your card out of sight.
Agree the amount aloud
Keep your card in your sight

ATM traps
Three traps to avoid
Never accept help at an ATM, even from someone who says he works there.
Stay at the machine. Call your bank's official number and block the card.
Loose, glued or extra-thick slot or keypad? Do not use that machine.
Use an ATM at a bank branch, in daylight. Never accept help from a stranger. If you need help, go inside the bank.
If the machine keeps your card, do not walk away. Call your bank's saved number from where you stand and block the card.
Before you insert your card, look at the slot and keypad. If anything looks loose or glued on, use another machine. And always take your card first, then your cash.
POS agent float
One morning's float
For example, Zainab runs a POS stand in Jos and starts with a float of 250,000 naira.
Cash after 3 customers
Agent account after 3 customers
Her own working numbers, not provider figures.
Float is cash in your drawer plus money in your agent account. Zainab starts with 150,000 cash and 100,000 in her account.
When a customer withdraws, her cash goes down and her account goes up. When a customer gives cash to send, the opposite happens.
After three customers she has 110,000 in cash and 140,000 in her account.
Still 250,000 in total. Her charges of 2,400 sit in a separate envelope, so she knows exactly what she earned.
Never give out cash until the terminal prints APPROVED and your app shows the credit.
When a payment fails
Debited but no cash
Do not repeat a failed payment. You may be debited twice.
Do not try the same payment again
Check your history for a reversal
Keep the receipt and references
Complain to your own bank, get a reference
For example, Ebere in Aba tries to withdraw 30,000 naira at a POS agent. It prints DECLINED, but she gets a debit alert. She does not let the agent try again.

That evening there is still no reversal, so she calls her own bank's number from the back of her card. Only your own bank can reverse a debit on your account. She writes down the complaint reference.
She checks daily until the 30,000 returns. If your bank does not resolve it, escalate within the bank, then to the CBN's consumer protection channel. Real banks never ask for your PIN or OTP.
